questions.q: Why couldn't 18th-century scientists determine the mass of the Earth directly from watching objects fall, even though they had Newton's law of universal gravitation?
options: Newton's law was known to be wrong at the time and gave impossible answers
A falling object only reveals the product of G and the Earth's mass, so the two unknowns could not be separated
They could not measure how fast objects fall with enough precision
The radius of the Earth had not yet been measured
questions.explanation: The acceleration of a falling stone depends on G multiplied by the Earth's mass as a single lump; measuring the fall only ever gives that product, so the two unknowns stay tangled together. Option 3 is wrong because the fall rate was measurable and precise measurement was not the barrier; the Earth's radius (option 4) was already known reasonably well.

questions.q: What was the central purpose of Cavendish's 1798 torsion-balance experiment?
options: To prove that gravity acts between all masses, not just between the Earth and objects
To measure the gravitational constant G by detecting the tiny attraction between lead balls in the laboratory
To measure the acceleration due to gravity, g, at the Earth's surface
To show that the Earth orbits the Sun
questions.explanation: By measuring the faint gravitational pull between masses on a tabletop, Cavendish could isolate G by itself. Option 3 is wrong because g was already known; the whole point was that g alone could not separate G from the Earth's mass. The experiment assumed universal gravitation (option 1) rather than trying to prove it.

questions.q: How does a torsion balance let you measure an extremely small force?
options: The fibre stretches downward in proportion to the weight hung on it
A twisted fibre exerts a restoring torque proportional to the angle of twist, so a tiny force produces a measurable rotation
The rod amplifies the force by acting as a long lever arm against gravity
The lead spheres become magnetised and repel one another
questions.explanation: The fibre resists twisting with a restoring torque equal to a wire constant times the twist angle, so even a whisper of a force twists it to a definite, measurable angle. Option 1 describes a spring balance under weight, not torsion; magnetism (option 4) plays no role, the effect is purely gravitational.

questions.q: At the point where the torsion balance settles and stops rotating, what is true?
options: The gravitational torque is much larger than the wire's restoring torque
The gravitational torque exactly equals the wire's restoring torque (zero net torque)
There is no gravitational force acting on the small spheres
The fibre has stopped exerting any torque
questions.explanation: The rod turns until the gravitational torque pulling it round is exactly balanced by the restoring torque of the twisted wire, giving zero net torque. Setting these equal (gravitational torque = k times theta) is what lets G be solved for. The forces do not vanish (options 3, 4); they are equal and opposite.

questions.q: How did Cavendish make a rotation far too small to see with the naked eye into a readable measurement?
options: He used a powerful microscope aimed directly at the fibre
He fixed a mirror to the balance and bounced a light beam onto a distant scale, so a tiny twist swept the spot a large distance
He timed how long the rod took to complete a full rotation
He weighed the deflected rod on a sensitive balance
questions.explanation: A mirror on the balance reflected a beam of light onto a scale far across the room; rotating the mirror by a hair sweeps the far end of the beam through a wide arc, optically amplifying the movement. This lever-of-light trick is why an invisible twist became a visible glide along a ruler.

questions.q: Why did Cavendish seal the apparatus in a case and observe it from another room through a telescope?
options: To keep the lead balls from being stolen
So that air draughts and his own body heat would not disturb a force barely stronger than nothing
Because the light beam could only be seen in total darkness
To let the fibre cool down between measurements
questions.explanation: The gravitational force he was measuring was so faint that a stray draught or the warmth of his own body could swamp the reading, so he isolated the apparatus and watched remotely. This obsessive control of confounding influences is what made the result trustworthy.

questions.q: Once Cavendish had a value for G on its own, what could immediately be worked out that had been impossible before?
options: The exact age of the Earth
The mass of the Earth, by dividing G out of the previously inseparable product of G and Earth's mass
The distance from the Earth to the Sun
The speed of light
questions.explanation: Gravity had always handed over G times the Earth's mass as one lump; knowing G alone let him divide it out and finally obtain the Earth's mass, effectively weighing the planet. The other quantities do not follow directly from G in this way.

questions.q: Cavendish was actually chasing the density of the Earth. What did his density result suggest about the planet's interior?
options: The Earth is uniform rock all the way through
The Earth is far denser than its surface rocks, hinting at something heavy such as iron at its core
The Earth is hollow
The Earth's core is made of water
questions.explanation: His result showed the planet was much denser than its crust, evidence for a heavy metallic (iron) core; the supplementary notes his density was about 80% that of liquid iron and 80% above the crust. A uniform rocky Earth would give a much lower average density.

questions.q: Cavendish's experiment yielded G = 6.74 x 10^-11 m^3 kg^-1 s^-2. The modern accepted value used in the HSC is 6.67 x 10^-11 m^3 kg^-1 s^-2. Calculate the percentage difference of Cavendish's value from the accepted value.
questions.given: Cavendish's value G = 6.74 x 10^-11; accepted value G = 6.67 x 10^-11 (both in m^3 kg^-1 s^-2)
questions.explanation: The difference of 0.07 x 10^-11 over the accepted 6.67 x 10^-11 gives about 1%. That an experiment done in 1798 with wood, wire and candlelight landed within roughly 1% of the value accepted over two centuries later shows the remarkable precision of Cavendish's method.

questions.q: Explain how Cavendish's torsion balance allowed the value of G to be extracted. Outline the balance of torques and which quantities were known versus measured.
keyPoints: Two large lead masses were placed near two small masses on the ends of a rod hung from a thin fibre, gravitationally pulling the rod round
The rod rotated until the gravitational torque was balanced by the wire's restoring torque (restoring torque = k times theta)
The wire constant k was determined beforehand (from the balance's oscillation period)
The twist angle theta was measured via the reflected light beam on a distant scale; the masses and separation distances were known
Setting gravitational torque equal to k times theta and rearranging leaves G as the only unknown, so it can be calculated
questions.explanation: At equilibrium the gravitational torque equals the restoring torque k times theta. Because k, the masses and the geometry are known and theta is measured, rearranging the balance equation isolates G. This is how a tabletop apparatus pinned down a fundamental constant of the universe.

questions.q: Why is measuring the gravitational constant G so significant for physics as a whole, beyond just weighing the Earth?
keyPoints: G is the constant that turns Newton's law of universal gravitation from a shape/relationship into an absolute scale
Without G, the masses of the Earth, Sun, planets and moons were all unknown because they depended on this one missing constant
With G known, we can weigh the Sun and distant planets just by watching how their gravity moves other objects
It lets us determine the mass of bodies we can never touch or reach
questions.explanation: G is the single number that gives Newton's law absolute magnitude; once it is known, every mass that expresses itself through gravity becomes calculable. Finding it once, on a tabletop, effectively gave the entire cosmos a set of scales.
